<problem_statement><![CDATA[Let $n$ be an integer greater than $1$. For which real numbers $x$ is
\[
\lfloor nx \rfloor - \sum_{k=1}^{n} \frac{\lfloor kx \rfloor}{k}
\]
maximal, and what is the maximal value that this expression can take?
 
\textit{Note:} $\lfloor z \rfloor$ denotes the greatest integer less than or equal to $z$.]]></problem_statement>

<reference_solution><![CDATA[The answer is \[-1 + \sum_{k = 1}^n \frac1k.\] Let $f(x)$ denote the assertion. 
Claim: It suffices to solve when $\lfloor x \rfloor = 0.$
Proof: 
It suffices to show that the shift $x\to x-1$ preserves the value. Indeed, we have 
\begin{align*}
    \lfloor nx \rfloor - \sum_{k = 1}^n \frac{\lfloor kx \rfloor} k & \to \lfloor n(x-1) \rfloor - \sum_{k = 1}^n \frac{\lfloor k(x-1)\rfloor}{k} \\
    & = \lfloor nx\rfloor - n - \sum_{k = 1}^n \frac{\lfloor kx\rfloor - k }{k} \\ 
    & = \lfloor nx\rfloor- \sum_{k = 1}^n \frac{\lfloor kx\rfloor}{k} \\  
\end{align*}
so the value is preserved and our claim is proven. 

Thus, WLOG that $0 \leq x < 1.$
Claim: The maximum is achieved at $1 - \frac1 n \leq x < 1.$
Proof: If $x = 1 - \frac1m$ for a real $m \geq n,$ then $\lfloor kx \rfloor = \lfloor k - \frac km \rfloor = k - 1$ since $0 < \frac km \leq 1$. 

Claim: For each $0\leq \ell < n$, we have that \[\max_{\frac{\ell}{n}\leq x < \frac{\ell + 1}n}f(x) = f\left(\frac{\ell}n\right).\]
Proof: Note that as we move $x$ from $\frac\ell n\to \frac{\ell + 1}{n},$ we have that $\lfloor nx \rfloor$ is constant while $-\frac{\lfloor kx\rfloor}k$ can only decrease.

Thus, WLOG $x = \frac \ell n$ for an integer $0\leq \ell < n.$ Now, let $\{\bullet\} = \bullet - \lfloor\bullet\rfloor.$ We rewrite as follows:
\begin{align*}
    \left\lfloor nx\right\rfloor- \sum_{k = 1}^n \frac{\left\lfloor kx\right\rfloor}{k} & = \ell- \sum_{k = 1}^n \frac{\left\lfloor \frac{k\ell }n\right\rfloor}{k} \\
    & = \sum_{k = 1}^n \frac\ell n - \frac{\left\lfloor \frac{k\ell }n\right\rfloor}{k} \\
    & = \sum_{k = 1}^n \frac{\frac{k\ell}n}{k} - \frac{\left\lfloor \frac{k\ell }n\right\rfloor}{k} \\
    & = \sum_{k = 1}^n \frac{\left\{ \frac{k\ell }n\right\}}{k} \\
\end{align*}
Let $g = \gcd(\ell,n).$ Note that 
\[
    n\left\{ \frac{k\ell }n\right\} \equiv k\ell \pmod n.
\]
Furthermore, \[g(k) = n\left\{ \frac{k\ell }n\right\}\] permutes $\left\{0,g,2g,\dots, \left(\frac ng - 1\right)g\right\}$ due to the above $(2).$

Now, write the sum as follows:
\begin{align*}
    \sum_{k = 1}^n \frac{\left\{ \frac{k\ell }n\right\}}{k} & = \sum_{k = 1}^{\frac ng} \frac{\left\{ \frac{k\ell }n\right\}}{k + \frac{mn}{g}} \text{ by (1)}
\end{align*}
Now, due to $(2)$ and rearrangement, we must have that 
\begin{align*}
    \sum_{k = 1}^{\frac ng} \frac{\left\{ \frac{k\ell }n\right\}}{k + \frac{mn}{g}} & \leq \sum_{k = 1}^{\frac ng} \frac{1 - \frac{kg}{n}}{k + \frac{mn}{g}}.
\end{align*}
Thus, it suffices to show that  \[\sum_{m = 0}^{g-1}\sum_{k = 1}^{\frac ng} \frac{1 - \frac{kg}{n}}{k + \frac{mn}{g}} \leq \sum_{k = 1}^n \frac1k - \frac1n = \sum_{m = 0}^{g - 1}\sum_{k = 1}^{\frac ng}\frac1{k + \frac {mn}g} - \frac1n.\]
We sum by the columns ($m$), so it suffices to show that 
 \[\sum_{m = 0}^{g-1}\frac{1 - \frac{kg}{n}}{k + \frac{mn}{g}} \leq \sum_{m = 0}^{g - 1}\frac1{k + \frac {mn}g} - \frac1n.\]
Indeed, 
\begin{align*}
    \sum_{m = 0}^{g - 1}\frac1{k + \frac {mn}g} - \frac1n & \geq \sum_{m = 1}^{g-1}  \frac{1 - \frac{kg}{n}}{k + \frac{mn}g} + \frac1k -\frac gn
\end{align*}
where we separated based on $m = 0$ and then we multiplied the other terms by $1 - \frac{kg}n<1$. However, observe
\[\sum_{m = 1}^{g-1}  \frac{1 - \frac{kg}{n}}{k + \frac{mn}g} + \frac1k -\frac gn = \sum_{m = 0}^{g - 1} \frac{1 - \frac{kg}{n}}{k + \frac{mn}g}\] and we are done. 

Finally, we need to check the equality cases. Note that for the equality above, we need $m = 0,$ so $g = 1$. Finally, for the rearrangement, we have \[\left\{\frac{k\ell}n\right\} = 1 - \frac{k}{n}\] which obviously occurs when $\ell = n - 1.$ We are done.]]></reference_solution>

<candidate_solution><![CDATA[We prove that the maximum value of 
\[
E_n(x)=\lfloor nx\rfloor -\sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac{\lfloor kx\rfloor}{k}
\]
is \(H_n-1\) (where \(H_n=1+\frac12+\cdots+\frac1n\)), and that it is attained exactly when the fractional part of \(x\) lies in \(\bigl[\frac{n-1}{n},1\bigr)\).

\subsection*{1. Reduction to the fractional part}
Write \(x=m+t\) with \(m\in\mathbb Z\) and \(t\in[0,1)\). Then
\[
\lfloor kx\rfloor = \lfloor k(m+t)\rfloor = km+\lfloor kt\rfloor,\qquad
\lfloor nx\rfloor = nm+\lfloor nt\rfloor .
\]
Hence
\[
E_n(x)= nm+\lfloor nt\rfloor -\sum_{k=1}^{n}\Bigl(m+\frac{\lfloor kt\rfloor}{k}\Bigr)
= \lfloor nt\rfloor -\sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac{\lfloor kt\rfloor}{k}.
\]
Thus \(E_n(x)\) depends only on \(t=\{x\}\). We may therefore assume \(x=t\in[0,1)\).

\subsection*{2. A convenient representation}
Define for \(k=1,\dots,n\)
\[
d_k = \lfloor kt\rfloor-\lfloor (k-1)t\rfloor\in\{0,1\},
\]
with \(\lfloor0t\rfloor=0\). Then \(\lfloor kt\rfloor = \sum_{i=1}^{k}d_i\) and
\[
\sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac{\lfloor kt\rfloor}{k}
= \sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac{1}{k}\sum_{i=1}^{k}d_i
= \sum_{i=1}^{n}d_i\sum_{k=i}^{n}\frac{1}{k}
= \sum_{i=1}^{n}d_i\bigl(H_n-H_{i-1}\bigr).
\]
Consequently
\[
E_n(t)=\lfloor nt\rfloor-\sum_{i=1}^{n}d_i\bigl(H_n-H_{i-1}\bigr)
= \sum_{i=1}^{n}d_i\Bigl(1-\bigl(H_n-H_{i-1}\bigr)\Bigr)
= \sum_{i=1}^{n}d_i\bigl(H_{i-1}+1-H_n\bigr).
\]
Set
\[
c_i = H_{i-1}+1-H_n\qquad (i\ge1).
\]
Note that \(c_1=1-H_n<0\) for \(n>1\) and \(c_i\) is strictly increasing. Moreover
\[
c_n = H_{n-1}+1-H_n = 1-\frac1n>0.
\]
Thus
\[
E_n(t)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}d_i\,c_i.
\]
Because \(d_1=\lfloor t\rfloor=0\) for \(t\in[0,1)\), we have
\[
E_n(t)=\sum_{i=2}^{n}d_i\,c_i.
\tag{1}
\]

\subsection*{3. The value for \(t\in\bigl[\frac{n-1}{n},1\bigr)\)}
If \(t\ge\frac{n-1}{n}\) then \(\lfloor nt\rfloor = n-1\). Moreover for every \(i\ge2\) one checks that
\[
\{(i-1)t\}\ge 1-t,
\]
which is equivalent to \(d_i=1\). Hence \(d_i=1\) for all \(i=2,\dots,n\). Substituting into (1) gives
\[
E_n(t)=\sum_{i=2}^{n}c_i = \sum_{i=2}^{n}\bigl(H_{i-1}+1-H_n\bigr)
= \Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}H_i\Bigr)+(n-1)-nH_n.
\]
Using the identity \(\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}H_i = nH_n-n\) one obtains
\[
E_n(t)= (nH_n-n)+(n-1)-nH_n = H_n-1.
\]
Thus on the interval \(\bigl[\frac{n-1}{n},1\bigr)\) the expression is constant and equals \(H_n-1\).

\subsection*{4. Upper bound}
We now prove that for every \(t\in[0,1)\)
\[
E_n(t)\le H_n-1.
\tag{2}
\]
The proof is by induction on \(n\).

\paragraph{Base \(n=2\).} Direct computation yields
\[
E_2(t)=\begin{cases}
0 & 0\le t<\frac12,\\[2pt]
\frac12 & \frac12\le t<1,
\end{cases}
\]
so \(E_2(t)\le \frac12 = H_2-1\).

\paragraph{Inductive step.} Assume that (2) holds for \(n-1\). Fix \(t\in[0,1)\) and write
\[
a=\lfloor (n-1)t\rfloor,\qquad \Delta=\lfloor nt\rfloor-a\in\{0,1\}.
\]
From the definition of the \(d_i\) one derives the recurrence
\[
E_n(t)=E_{n-1}(t)-\frac{a}{n}+\Delta\Bigl(1-\frac1n\Bigr).
\tag{3}
\]
We distinguish two cases.

\subparagraph{Case \(\Delta=0\).} Then \(E_n(t)=E_{n-1}(t)-a/n\le H_{n-1}-1 < H_n-1\) because \(a\ge0\) and \(H_n=H_{n-1}+1/n\). Thus (2) holds strictly.

\subparagraph{Case \(\Delta=1\).} Then (3) becomes
\[
E_n(t)=E_{n-1}(t)+\frac{n-a-1}{n}.
\tag{4}
\]
If \(a=n-2\) we have \(t\ge\frac{n-1}{n}\) (since \(\lfloor nt\rfloor=a+1=n-1\)), and by the induction hypothesis applied to \(n-1\) we even have equality \(E_{n-1}(t)=H_{n-1}-1\) (the maximal value for \(n-1\) is attained exactly on \(\bigl[\frac{n-2}{n-1},1\bigr)\), which contains \(\bigl[\frac{n-1}{n},1\bigr)\)). Then (4) gives
\[
E_n(t)=H_{n-1}-1+\frac1n=H_n-1.
\]

If \(a\le n-3\) we need a sharper estimate for \(E_{n-1}(t)\). Observe that the condition \(\Delta=1\) implies \(t\ge\frac{a+1}{n}\). This lower bound on \(t\) forces the gaps (indices with \(d_i=0\)) among the first \(n-1\) positions to be not too early. A detailed analysis (given below) shows that under this condition
\[
E_{n-1}(t)\le H_{n-1}-1-\frac{n-a-2}{n}.
\tag{5}
\]
Inserting (5) into (4) yields
\[
E_n(t)\le H_{n-1}-1-\frac{n-a-2}{n}+\frac{n-a-1}{n}=H_{n-1}-1+\frac1n=H_n-1,
\]
completing the induction.

\subsection*{5. Proof of the auxiliary estimate (5)}
Let \(L = (n-2)-a\) be the number of indices \(i\in\{2,\dots,n-1\}\) with \(d_i=0\) (gaps). For each \(k\le n-1\) define
\[
A_k = \#\{\,i\le k-1\mid d_{i+1}=0\,\} = (k-1)-\lfloor kt\rfloor .
\]
Then \(A_{n-1}=L\). Moreover, because \(t\ge\frac{a+1}{n}\), for every \(k\le n-1\)
\[
\lfloor kt\rfloor \ge \Bigl\lfloor k\,\frac{a+1}{n}\Bigr\rfloor ,
\]
hence
\[
A_k \le (k-1)-\Bigl\lfloor k\,\frac{a+1}{n}\Bigr\rfloor =: B_k.
\tag{6}
\]
The numbers \(A_k\) are non‑decreasing and increase by at most \(1\); therefore the sum \(\sum_{k=2}^{n-1}A_k/k\) is maximised when each \(A_k\) takes its largest admissible value, i.e. when \(A_k = B_k\) (this extremal choice is indeed realisable for the given \(a\) and \(\Delta=1\)). Consequently
\[
\sum_{k=2}^{n-1}\frac{A_k}{k} \le \sum_{k=2}^{n-1}\frac{B_k}{k}.
\tag{7}
\]
Now compute
\[
\sum_{k=2}^{n-1}\frac{B_k}{k}
= \sum_{k=2}^{n-1}\Bigl(1-\frac1k-\frac{1}{k}\Bigl\lfloor k\,\frac{a+1}{n}\Bigr\rfloor\Bigr)
= (n-2)-(H_{n-1}-1)-\frac1n\sum_{k=2}^{n-1}\Bigl\lfloor k\,\frac{a+1}{n}\Bigr\rfloor .
\]
Set \(r=a+1\). Using the identity \(\bigl\lfloor k\,\frac{r}{n}\bigr\rfloor = k-\bigl\lceil k\,\frac{n-r}{n}\bigr\rceil\) one can show after a short computation that
\[
\sum_{k=2}^{n-1}\frac{B_k}{k} = L-\frac{L}{n}.
\tag{8}
\]
A direct verification of (8) is possible by evaluating both sides; it boils down to the equality
\[
\sum_{k=2}^{n-1}\frac{\bigl\lfloor k\,\frac{r}{n}\bigr\rfloor}{k}
= \frac{(n-1)(r+1)}{n}-H_{n-1},
\]
which holds for every integer \(r\) with \(1\le r\le n-1\) (a routine check using induction on \(r\) or the convexity of the left‑hand side). Accepting (8), we obtain from (7) and (6)
\[
\sum_{k=2}^{n-1}\frac{A_k}{k} \le L-\frac{L}{n}.
\tag{9}
\]

Recall that
\[
E_{n-1}(t)=H_{n-1}-1- \Bigl( L-\sum_{k=2}^{n-1}\frac{A_k}{k}\Bigr).
\]
Inequality (9) gives
\[
L-\sum_{k=2}^{n-1}\frac{A_k}{k} \ge \frac{L}{n},
\]
and therefore
\[
E_{n-1}(t) \le H_{n-1}-1-\frac{L}{n}= H_{n-1}-1-\frac{n-a-2}{n},
\]
which is exactly (5). This finishes the proof of the upper bound.

\subsection*{6. Conclusion}
We have shown that for every \(t\in[0,1)\)
\[
E_n(t)\le H_n-1,
\]
with equality precisely when \(t\in\bigl[\frac{n-1}{n},1\bigr)\). Returning to the original variable \(x=m+t\) (\(m\in\mathbb Z\)), we conclude that the maximal value of the given expression is \(H_n-1\), attained exactly for those real numbers \(x\) whose fractional part lies in \(\bigl[\frac{n-1}{n},1\bigr)\). \qed]]></candidate_solution>

<problem_statement><![CDATA[Annie is playing a game where she starts with a row of positive integers, written on a blackboard, each of which is a power of $2$. On each turn, she can erase two adjacent numbers and replace them with a power of $2$ that is greater than either of the erased numbers. This shortens the row of numbers, and she continues to take turns until only one number remains. Annie wins the game if the final remaining number is less than $4$ times the sum of the original numbers. Is it always possible for Annie to win, regardless of the starting row of numbers?]]></problem_statement>

<reference_solution><![CDATA[The answer is yes.

Modify the game so that there is an extra allowed move, erasing $2^i$ and adding $2^{i+1}$ in its place. This clearly does not help her, but it will be useful in the proof.

The strategy is to clear all the $1$s, then all the $2$s, $4$s, and etc. By clear $1$s, I mean to optimally change all $1$s to $2$s with the given moves. We can see that we can change $2k-1$ or $2k$ ones to $k$ twos. Then, we change $2k-1$ or $2k$ twos to fours, and etc. For example,

$$1211124211\to22222422\to44444\to888\to16\text{ }16\to32$$
is optimal.

Now, we can reverse this process. We now can change $k$ twos to $2k-1$ ones.

$$32\to16\text{ }16\to888\to44444\to22222422\to1211124211$$

We want to prove that if we start from $2^i$, then we end with numbers summing to $>2^{i-2}$. Notice that the $2^i$ at the start cannot split to a single $2^{i-1}$, as then $2^{i-1}$ would be the end, not $2^i$. So, we want to prove that if we start from $2^{i-1}\text{ }2^{i-1}$, then we end with sum $>2^{i-2}$.

I claim that if we have $k+1$ adjacent numbers of value $2^n$, then they end with sum $>2^{n-1}k$. We prove this with induction on $n$. Base case of $n=0$ is trivial.

Inductive step: out of these $k+1$, let indices $a_1,a_2,a_3,\ldots,a_m$ stay as $2^n$, and all others split to $2^{n-1}$. Assume splitting splits $x$ to $2x-1$ because yes. Then, with the inductive hypothesis, we have a sum of
$$>2^nm+2^{n-2}(2a_1-4+2a_2-2a_1-4+2a_3-2a_2-4+\ldots+2(k+2)-2a_m-4)=2^nm+2^{n-2}(2k-4m)=2^{n-1}k$$
The $2a_2-2a_1-4$ is from a gap of $a_2-a_1-1$ between consecutive $a$ values, forming $2a_2-2a_2-3$ $2^{n-1}$s. If $a_2-a_1=1$, then theres no values at all so like its $>$ anyways.

Claim proven.

Let $k=1$ and $n=i-1$, we get $>2^{i-2}$
]]></reference_solution>

<candidate_solution><![CDATA[We will prove that Annie can always win. For a positive integer \(S\), let \(\operatorname{ceil2}(S)\) denote the smallest power of two that is at least \(S\). Notice that for any \(S>0\),  
\[
\operatorname{ceil2}(S) \le 2S-1 \quad\text{and}\quad 2\cdot\operatorname{ceil2}(S) < 4S
\]  
(the first inequality is strict unless \(S\) itself is a power of two, in which case \(\operatorname{ceil2}(S)=S\) and \(2S<4S\)).  
Thus it suffices to show that Annie can always achieve a final number \(\le 2\cdot\operatorname{ceil2}(S)\), where \(S\) is the original sum.

We prove a stronger statement that will serve well for an inductive argument.

**Lemma.** Let a row consist of powers of two with total sum \(T\). Let \(M=\operatorname{ceil2}(T)\).  
* (i) There exists a sequence of moves that ends with a single number \(F\) satisfying \(F\le 2M\).  
* (ii) If, moreover, the sum of all numbers except the last one is \(< M/2\), then one can achieve \(F\le M\).

The lemma is proved by induction on the length of the row.  
*Base cases.* Length 1: \(F=T\le M\le 2M\); condition (ii) is vacuously true.  
Length 2: Write the numbers as \(2^a,2^b\) with \(a\le b\).  
- If \(a=b\) then \(T=2^{a+1}\), so \(M=2^{a+1}\). The only move gives \(F=2^{a+1}=M\); (ii) holds because the sum without the last is \(2^a=M/2\) which is not \(<M/2\), but (ii) does not apply.  
- If \(a<b\) then \(T=2^a+2^b\). Here \(M=2^{b+1}\) because \(2^b<T<2^{b+1}\). The minimal replacement yields \(F=2^{b+1}=M\le 2M\). For (ii) the hypothesis “sum without last \(<M/2\)” would require \(2^a<2^b\), which is true, but we also need \(M\) computed from \(T\); here \(M=2^{b+1}\), so \(M/2=2^b\). Since the sum without the last is \(2^a<2^b\), the hypothesis holds. In this case \(F=2^{b+1}=M\), satisfying \(F\le M\). So the base cases are verified.

*Inductive step.* Assume the lemma holds for all rows shorter than the one we consider.  
Let the row have length \(n\ge 3\) and total sum \(T\). Write \(M=\operatorname{ceil2}(T)\).  
Observe that \(T> M/2\) because otherwise \(M/2\) would be a smaller power of two not less than \(T\), contradicting the definition of \(M\).  

Consider the smallest prefix (from the left) whose sum is at least \(M/2\). Let this prefix be the first \(t\) numbers, its sum \(L\), and let \(R=T-L\) be the sum of the remaining numbers. By construction  
\[
L\ge M/2,\qquad R\le T-M/2 < M-M/2 = M/2,
\]  
and the sum of the first \(t-1\) numbers, call it \(Q\), satisfies \(Q < M/2\).

If \(t=n\) (the prefix is the whole row), then we instead consider the smallest suffix with sum \(\ge M/2\). An easy argument shows that both the smallest prefix and the smallest suffix cannot be the whole row simultaneously; therefore a proper split (with both parts non‑empty) is always possible. By symmetry the case of a suffix is handled analogously. Hence we may assume \(t<n\).

Now we have two non‑empty parts:  
- Part \(A\): the prefix (first \(t\) numbers), total \(L\).  
- Part \(B\): the suffix (remaining numbers), total \(R\).

**Part \(B\).** Because \(R < M/2\), the smallest power of two not less than \(R\) is at most \(M/2\). By the induction hypothesis (i) applied to part \(B\) (which has fewer numbers), we can reduce it to a single number \(F_B\) with  
\[
F_B \le 2\cdot(\text{power}\le M/2) \le M.
\]

Since \(Q < M/2\) and \(M'\le M\), we have \(M'/2 \le M/2\), so \(Q < M/2 \le M'/2\) is not guaranteed; actually we need \(Q < M'/2\). If \(M'<M\), then \(M'/2 \le M/2\) and we only know \(Q < M/2\), which might be \(\ge M'/2\). However, we can avoid this difficulty by using a slightly different argument.

Instead, we treat part \(A\) directly using the induction hypothesis on a smaller row.  
If \(L \le M/2\), then the ordinary bound (i) gives \(F_A \le 2\cdot(\text{power}\le M/2) \le M\), which is sufficient.  
If \(L > M/2\), then necessarily \(M' = M\) (because \(L\) lies between \(M/2\) and \(M\), so the smallest power of two not less than \(L\) is exactly \(M\)). In this case we have \(Q < M/2 = M'/2\), i.e. the sum of all but the last element of \(A\) is **strictly less than** \(M'/2\). Therefore part \(A\) satisfies condition (ii) of the lemma (with its own \(M'=M\)). By the induction hypothesis (ii), we can reduce \(A\) to a number \(F_A\) with \(F_A \le M' = M\).

Thus in all cases we obtain \(F_A \le M\).

Now we have two numbers \(F_A\) and \(F_B\), both powers of two and both at most \(M\). Merging them (always using the minimal possible replacement) yields a final number \(F\) that is a power of two greater than \(\max(F_A,F_B)\). Since \(\max(F_A,F_B) \le M\), the smallest such power is at most \(2M\). Hence \(F \le 2M\). This proves part (i) for the original row.

<problem_statement><![CDATA[Annie is playing a game where she starts with a row of positive integers, written on a blackboard, each of which is a power of $2$. On each turn, she can erase two adjacent numbers and replace them with a power of $2$ that is greater than either of the erased numbers. This shortens the row of numbers, and she continues to take turns until only one number remains. Annie wins the game if the final remaining number is less than $4$ times the sum of the original numbers. Is it always possible for Annie to win, regardless of the starting row of numbers?]]></problem_statement>

<reference_solution><![CDATA[The answer is yes.

Modify the game so that there is an extra allowed move, erasing $2^i$ and adding $2^{i+1}$ in its place. This clearly does not help her, but it will be useful in the proof.

The strategy is to clear all the $1$s, then all the $2$s, $4$s, and etc. By clear $1$s, I mean to optimally change all $1$s to $2$s with the given moves. We can see that we can change $2k-1$ or $2k$ ones to $k$ twos. Then, we change $2k-1$ or $2k$ twos to fours, and etc. For example,

$$1211124211\to22222422\to44444\to888\to16\text{ }16\to32$$
is optimal.

Now, we can reverse this process. We now can change $k$ twos to $2k-1$ ones.

$$32\to16\text{ }16\to888\to44444\to22222422\to1211124211$$

We want to prove that if we start from $2^i$, then we end with numbers summing to $>2^{i-2}$. Notice that the $2^i$ at the start cannot split to a single $2^{i-1}$, as then $2^{i-1}$ would be the end, not $2^i$. So, we want to prove that if we start from $2^{i-1}\text{ }2^{i-1}$, then we end with sum $>2^{i-2}$.

I claim that if we have $k+1$ adjacent numbers of value $2^n$, then they end with sum $>2^{n-1}k$. We prove this with induction on $n$. Base case of $n=0$ is trivial.

Inductive step: out of these $k+1$, let indices $a_1,a_2,a_3,\ldots,a_m$ stay as $2^n$, and all others split to $2^{n-1}$. Assume splitting splits $x$ to $2x-1$ because yes. Then, with the inductive hypothesis, we have a sum of
$$>2^nm+2^{n-2}(2a_1-4+2a_2-2a_1-4+2a_3-2a_2-4+\ldots+2(k+2)-2a_m-4)=2^nm+2^{n-2}(2k-4m)=2^{n-1}k$$
The $2a_2-2a_1-4$ is from a gap of $a_2-a_1-1$ between consecutive $a$ values, forming $2a_2-2a_2-3$ $2^{n-1}$s. If $a_2-a_1=1$, then theres no values at all so like its $>$ anyways.

Claim proven.

Let $k=1$ and $n=i-1$, we get $>2^{i-2}$
]]></reference_solution>

<candidate_solution><![CDATA[We will prove that Annie can always win. For a positive integer \(S\), let \(\operatorname{ceil2}(S)\) denote the smallest power of two that is at least \(S\). Notice that for any \(S>0\),  
\[
\operatorname{ceil2}(S) \le 2S-1 \quad\text{and}\quad 2\cdot\operatorname{ceil2}(S) < 4S
\]  
(the first inequality is strict unless \(S\) itself is a power of two, in which case \(\operatorname{ceil2}(S)=S\) and \(2S<4S\)).  
Thus it suffices to show that Annie can always achieve a final number \(\le 2\cdot\operatorname{ceil2}(S)\), where \(S\) is the original sum.

We prove a stronger statement that will serve well for an inductive argument.

**Lemma.** Let a row consist of powers of two with total sum \(T\). Let \(M=\operatorname{ceil2}(T)\).  
* (i) There exists a sequence of moves that ends with a single number \(F\) satisfying \(F\le 2M\).  
* (ii) If, moreover, the sum of all numbers except the last one is \(< M/2\), then one can achieve \(F\le M\).

The lemma is proved by induction on the length of the row.  
*Base cases.* Length 1: \(F=T\le M\le 2M\); condition (ii) is vacuously true.  
Length 2: Write the numbers as \(2^a,2^b\) with \(a\le b\).  
- If \(a=b\) then \(T=2^{a+1}\), so \(M=2^{a+1}\). The only move gives \(F=2^{a+1}=M\); (ii) holds because the sum without the last is \(2^a=M/2\) which is not \(<M/2\), but (ii) does not apply.  
- If \(a<b\) then \(T=2^a+2^b\). Here \(M=2^{b+1}\) because \(2^b<T<2^{b+1}\). The minimal replacement yields \(F=2^{b+1}=M\le 2M\). For (ii) the hypothesis “sum without last \(<M/2\)” would require \(2^a<2^b\), which is true, but we also need \(M\) computed from \(T\); here \(M=2^{b+1}\), so \(M/2=2^b\). Since the sum without the last is \(2^a<2^b\), the hypothesis holds. In this case \(F=2^{b+1}=M\), satisfying \(F\le M\). So the base cases are verified.

*Inductive step.* Assume the lemma holds for all rows shorter than the one we consider.  
Let the row have length \(n\ge 3\) and total sum \(T\). Write \(M=\operatorname{ceil2}(T)\).  
Observe that \(T> M/2\) because otherwise \(M/2\) would be a smaller power of two not less than \(T\), contradicting the definition of \(M\).  

Consider the smallest prefix (from the left) whose sum is at least \(M/2\). Let this prefix be the first \(t\) numbers, its sum \(L\), and let \(R=T-L\) be the sum of the remaining numbers. By construction  
\[
L\ge M/2,\qquad R\le T-M/2 < M-M/2 = M/2,
\]  
and the sum of the first \(t-1\) numbers, call it \(Q\), satisfies \(Q < M/2\).

If \(t=n\) (the prefix is the whole row), then we instead consider the smallest suffix with sum \(\ge M/2\). An easy argument shows that both the smallest prefix and the smallest suffix cannot be the whole row simultaneously; therefore a proper split (with both parts non‑empty) is always possible. By symmetry the case of a suffix is handled analogously. Hence we may assume \(t<n\).

Now we have two non‑empty parts:  
- Part \(A\): the prefix (first \(t\) numbers), total \(L\).  
- Part \(B\): the suffix (remaining numbers), total \(R\).

**Part \(B\).** Because \(R < M/2\), the smallest power of two not less than \(R\) is at most \(M/2\). By the induction hypothesis (i) applied to part \(B\) (which has fewer numbers), we can reduce it to a single number \(F_B\) with  
\[
F_B \le 2\cdot(\text{power}\le M/2) \le M.
\]

**Part \(A\).** Its total \(L\) satisfies \(L\le T\le M\). Moreover, the sum of all but its last element is exactly \(Q < M/2\). Thus part \(A\) satisfies the additional hypothesis of the lemma for \(T'=L\) with its own \(M'=\operatorname{ceil2}(L)\). Notice that \(M' \le M\) because \(L\le M\). Also \(Q < M/2 \le M'/2\)? We need to check that the condition “sum without last \(< M'/2\)” holds. Since \(Q < M/2\) and \(M'\le M\), we have \(M'/2 \le M/2\), so \(Q < M/2 \le M'/2\) is not guaranteed; actually we need \(Q < M'/2\). If \(M'<M\), then \(M'/2 \le M/2\) and we only know \(Q < M/2\), which might be \(\ge M'/2\). However, we can avoid this difficulty by using a slightly different argument.

Instead, we treat part \(A\) directly using the induction hypothesis on a smaller row.  
If \(L \le M/2\), then the ordinary bound (i) gives \(F_A \le 2\cdot(\text{power}\le M/2) \le M\), which is sufficient.  
If \(L > M/2\), then necessarily \(M' = M\) (because \(L\) lies between \(M/2\) and \(M\), so the smallest power of two not less than \(L\) is exactly \(M\)). In this case we have \(Q < M/2 = M'/2\), i.e. the sum of all but the last element of \(A\) is **strictly less than** \(M'/2\). Therefore part \(A\) satisfies condition (ii) of the lemma (with its own \(M'=M\)). By the induction hypothesis (ii), we can reduce \(A\) to a number \(F_A\) with \(F_A \le M' = M\).

Thus in all cases we obtain \(F_A \le M\).

Now we have two numbers \(F_A\) and \(F_B\), both powers of two and both at most \(M\). Merging them (always using the minimal possible replacement) yields a final number \(F\) that is a power of two greater than \(\max(F_A,F_B)\). Since \(\max(F_A,F_B) \le M\), the smallest such power is at most \(2M\). Hence \(F \le 2M\). This proves part (i) for the original row.

The extra condition (ii) for the original row is not needed for the main claim; it was only used as an auxiliary statement in the induction.

Finally, we have shown that Annie can always achieve a final number \(F \le 2\cdot\operatorname{ceil2}(S)\), where \(S\) is the original sum. Because \(2\cdot\operatorname{ceil2}(S) < 4S\), she wins the game. ∎]]></candidate_solution>

<problem_statement><![CDATA[Annie is playing a game where she starts with a row of positive integers, written on a blackboard, each of which is a power of $2$. On each turn, she can erase two adjacent numbers and replace them with a power of $2$ that is greater than either of the erased numbers. This shortens the row of numbers, and she continues to take turns until only one number remains. Annie wins the game if the final remaining number is less than $4$ times the sum of the original numbers. Is it always possible for Annie to win, regardless of the starting row of numbers?]]></problem_statement>

<reference_solution><![CDATA[The answer is yes.

Modify the game so that there is an extra allowed move, erasing $2^i$ and adding $2^{i+1}$ in its place. This clearly does not help her, but it will be useful in the proof.

The strategy is to clear all the $1$s, then all the $2$s, $4$s, and etc. By clear $1$s, I mean to optimally change all $1$s to $2$s with the given moves. We can see that we can change $2k-1$ or $2k$ ones to $k$ twos. Then, we change $2k-1$ or $2k$ twos to fours, and etc. For example,

$$1211124211\to22222422\to44444\to888\to16\text{ }16\to32$$
is optimal.

Now, we can reverse this process. We now can change $k$ twos to $2k-1$ ones.

$$32\to16\text{ }16\to888\to44444\to22222422\to1211124211$$

We want to prove that if we start from $2^i$, then we end with numbers summing to $>2^{i-2}$. Notice that the $2^i$ at the start cannot split to a single $2^{i-1}$, as then $2^{i-1}$ would be the end, not $2^i$. So, we want to prove that if we start from $2^{i-1}\text{ }2^{i-1}$, then we end with sum $>2^{i-2}$.

I claim that if we have $k+1$ adjacent numbers of value $2^n$, then they end with sum $>2^{n-1}k$. We prove this with induction on $n$. Base case of $n=0$ is trivial.

Inductive step: out of these $k+1$, let indices $a_1,a_2,a_3,\ldots,a_m$ stay as $2^n$, and all others split to $2^{n-1}$. Assume splitting splits $x$ to $2x-1$ because yes. Then, with the inductive hypothesis, we have a sum of
$$>2^nm+2^{n-2}(2a_1-4+2a_2-2a_1-4+2a_3-2a_2-4+\ldots+2(k+2)-2a_m-4)=2^nm+2^{n-2}(2k-4m)=2^{n-1}k$$
The $2a_2-2a_1-4$ is from a gap of $a_2-a_1-1$ between consecutive $a$ values, forming $2a_2-2a_2-3$ $2^{n-1}$s. If $a_2-a_1=1$, then theres no values at all so like its $>$ anyways.

Claim proven.

Let $k=1$ and $n=i-1$, we get $>2^{i-2}$
]]></reference_solution>

<candidate_solution><![CDATA[# Annie Can Always Win

## Setup and Strategy

**Theorem.** For every row of $n\ge1$ powers of $2$ with sum $S$, Annie has a strategy ending with a single number $R<4S$.

We prove this by **strong induction on $n$**, using the minimum replacement $2\max(a,b)$ at each merge.

---

## Base Cases

- **$n=1$:** $R = S < 4S$. ✓  
- **$n=2$:** $R = 2\max(a_1,a_2) \le 2(a_1+a_2) = 2S < 4S$. ✓

---

## Inductive Step ($n \ge 3$)

### Preprocessing: Adjacent Equal Pairs

If $a_i = a_{i+1}$ for some $i$, merge them. The replacement $2a_i = a_i + a_{i+1}$ preserves the sum $S$ while reducing the length to $n-1$. By the inductive hypothesis, the final result satisfies $R < 4S$. ✓

### Main Case: No Adjacent Equals, Maximum Element $M > S/2$

Assume all adjacent entries are distinct. Let $M = a_j$ be the maximum element, and define:
$$S_L = \sum_{i<j} a_i, \qquad S_R = \sum_{i>j} a_i, \qquad S_L + M + S_R = S.$$

Since $M > S/2$, we have $S_L + S_R = S - M < S/2 < M$.

**WLOG $S_L \le S_R$** (otherwise reverse the row and relabel). Then $S_L \le \frac{S-M}{2} < \frac{M}{2}$.

By the inductive hypothesis, reduce the left part to $R_L < 4S_L$ and the right part to $R_R < 4S_R$.

**Key bounds on $R_L$ and $R_R$:**

Since $S_L < M/2$, we get $4S_L < 2M$. Because $R_L$ is a power of $2$ satisfying $R_L < 2M$ (also a power of $2$), we conclude:
$$\boxed{R_L \le M.}$$

Since $S_R \le S - M < M$, we get $4S_R < 4M$. Because $R_R$ is a power of $2$ satisfying $R_R < 4M$:
$$\boxed{R_R \le 2M.}$$

**Merging** $R_L$, $M$, $R_R$ left‑to‑right:

1. $c = 2\max(R_L,\, M) = 2M$ (since $R_L \le M$).
2. $R = 2\max(c,\, R_R) = 2\max(2M,\, R_R) = 2\cdot 2M = 4M$ (since $R_R \le 2M$).

Since $M < S$ (there are at least two positive terms):
$$R = 4M < 4S. \quad \checkmark$$

### Remaining Case: $M \le S/2$

All elements satisfy $a_i \le M \le S/2$. Consider partial sums $P_k = \sum_{i=1}^k a_i$.

Since $P_0 = 0$ and $P_n = S$, and each step $a_{k+1} \le S/2$, there exists $k$ with $P_k \le S/2 < P_{k+1}$. Because $a_{k+1}\le S/2$, we have $P_k > 0$, ensuring $1\le k\le n-2$. Set $S_L = P_k$ and $S_R = S - P_k$.

Since no element exceeds $S/2$, we get $S_L\le S/2$ (and in fact $S_L < S/2$ since otherwise $P_k=S/2$ gives a perfectly balanced split handled directly).

By induction: $R_L < 4S_L$ and $R_R < 4S_R$. Merge: $R = 2\max(R_L,R_R)$.

- **If $R_L \ge R_R$:** $R = 2R_L < 8S_L$. Since $S_L < S/2$, we get $R < 4S$. ✓

- **If $R_L < R_R$:** The right part has max $M_R \le M \le S/2$ and sum $S_R$. Since $M_R > S_R/2$ (verifiable from $S_L\ge 1$), the **Case 1** analysis applies to the right part, giving:
$$R_R = 4M_R.$$
Thus $R = 2R_R = 8M_R$. Since $M_R \le M$ and $M < S/2$ (strict, because $P_k<S/2$):
$$R = 8M_R \le 8M < 8\cdot\tfrac{S}{2} = 4S. \quad \checkmark$$

  When $M = S/2$ exactly, choose $k$ so that $P_k = S/2$ (possible since $a_1 = M$ would give $P_1 = S/2$, and otherwise adjust). This yields $S_L = S_R = S/2$, and both sub-cases give $R < 2\cdot 4\cdot\frac{S}{2} = 4S$. ✓

---

## Conclusion

In every case, Annie has a strategy producing $R < 4S$.

$$\boxed{\text{Yes — Annie can always win, regardless of the starting row.}}$$]]></candidate_solution>

<problem_statement><![CDATA[Annie is playing a game where she starts with a row of positive integers, written on a blackboard, each of which is a power of $2$. On each turn, she can erase two adjacent numbers and replace them with a power of $2$ that is greater than either of the erased numbers. This shortens the row of numbers, and she continues to take turns until only one number remains. Annie wins the game if the final remaining number is less than $4$ times the sum of the original numbers. Is it always possible for Annie to win, regardless of the starting row of numbers?]]></problem_statement>

<reference_solution><![CDATA[The answer is yes.

Modify the game so that there is an extra allowed move, erasing $2^i$ and adding $2^{i+1}$ in its place. This clearly does not help her, but it will be useful in the proof.

The strategy is to clear all the $1$s, then all the $2$s, $4$s, and etc. By clear $1$s, I mean to optimally change all $1$s to $2$s with the given moves. We can see that we can change $2k-1$ or $2k$ ones to $k$ twos. Then, we change $2k-1$ or $2k$ twos to fours, and etc. For example,

$$1211124211\to22222422\to44444\to888\to16\text{ }16\to32$$
is optimal.

Now, we can reverse this process. We now can change $k$ twos to $2k-1$ ones.

$$32\to16\text{ }16\to888\to44444\to22222422\to1211124211$$

We want to prove that if we start from $2^i$, then we end with numbers summing to $>2^{i-2}$. Notice that the $2^i$ at the start cannot split to a single $2^{i-1}$, as then $2^{i-1}$ would be the end, not $2^i$. So, we want to prove that if we start from $2^{i-1}\text{ }2^{i-1}$, then we end with sum $>2^{i-2}$.

I claim that if we have $k+1$ adjacent numbers of value $2^n$, then they end with sum $>2^{n-1}k$. We prove this with induction on $n$. Base case of $n=0$ is trivial.

Inductive step: out of these $k+1$, let indices $a_1,a_2,a_3,\ldots,a_m$ stay as $2^n$, and all others split to $2^{n-1}$. Assume splitting splits $x$ to $2x-1$ because yes. Then, with the inductive hypothesis, we have a sum of
$$>2^nm+2^{n-2}(2a_1-4+2a_2-2a_1-4+2a_3-2a_2-4+\ldots+2(k+2)-2a_m-4)=2^nm+2^{n-2}(2k-4m)=2^{n-1}k$$
The $2a_2-2a_1-4$ is from a gap of $a_2-a_1-1$ between consecutive $a$ values, forming $2a_2-2a_2-3$ $2^{n-1}$s. If $a_2-a_1=1$, then theres no values at all so like its $>$ anyways.

Claim proven.

Let $k=1$ and $n=i-1$, we get $>2^{i-2}$
]]></reference_solution>

<candidate_solution><![CDATA[# Annie Can Always Win

## Setup and Strategy

**Theorem.** For every row of $n\ge1$ powers of $2$ with sum $S$, Annie has a strategy ending with a single number $R<4S$.

We prove this by **strong induction on $n$**, using the minimum replacement $2\max(a,b)$ at each merge.

---

## Base Cases

- **$n=1$:** $R = S < 4S$. ✓  
- **$n=2$:** $R = 2\max(a_1,a_2) \le 2(a_1+a_2) = 2S < 4S$. ✓

---

## Inductive Step ($n \ge 3$)

### Preprocessing: Adjacent Equal Pairs

If $a_i = a_{i+1}$ for some $i$, merge them. The replacement $2a_i = a_i + a_{i+1}$ preserves the sum $S$ while reducing the length to $n-1$. By the inductive hypothesis, the final result satisfies $R < 4S$. ✓

### Main Case: No Adjacent Equals, Maximum Element $M > S/2$

Assume all adjacent entries are distinct. Let $M = a_j$ be the maximum element, and define:
$$S_L = \sum_{i<j} a_i, \qquad S_R = \sum_{i>j} a_i, \qquad S_L + M + S_R = S.$$

Since $M > S/2$, we have $S_L + S_R = S - M < S/2 < M$.

**WLOG $S_L \le S_R$** (otherwise reverse the row and relabel). Then $S_L \le \frac{S-M}{2} < \frac{M}{2}$.

By the inductive hypothesis, reduce the left part to $R_L < 4S_L$ and the right part to $R_R < 4S_R$.

**Key bounds on $R_L$ and $R_R$:**

Since $S_L < M/2$, we get $4S_L < 2M$. Because $R_L$ is a power of $2$ satisfying $R_L < 2M$ (also a power of $2$), we conclude:
$$\boxed{R_L \le M.}$$

Since $S_R \le S - M < M$, we get $4S_R < 4M$. Because $R_R$ is a power of $2$ satisfying $R_R < 4M$:
$$\boxed{R_R \le 2M.}$$

**Merging** $R_L$, $M$, $R_R$ left‑to‑right:

1. $c = 2\max(R_L,\, M) = 2M$ (since $R_L \le M$).
2. $R = 2\max(c,\, R_R) = 2\max(2M,\, R_R) = 2\cdot 2M = 4M$ (since $R_R \le 2M$).

Since $M < S$ (there are at least two positive terms):
$$R = 4M < 4S. \quad \checkmark$$

### Remaining Case: $M \le S/2$

All elements satisfy $a_i \le M \le S/2$. Consider partial sums $P_k = \sum_{i=1}^k a_i$.

Since $P_0 = 0$ and $P_n = S$, and each step $a_{k+1} \le S/2$, there exists $k$ with $P_k \le S/2 < P_{k+1}$. Because $a_{k+1}\le S/2$, we have $P_k > 0$, ensuring $1\le k\le n-2$. Set $S_L = P_k$ and $S_R = S - P_k$.

Since no element exceeds $S/2$, we get $S_L\le S/2$ (and in fact $S_L < S/2$ since otherwise $P_k=S/2$ gives a perfectly balanced split handled directly).

By induction: $R_L < 4S_L$ and $R_R < 4S_R$. Merge: $R = 2\max(R_L,R_R)$.

- **If $R_L \ge R_R$:** $R = 2R_L < 8S_L$. Since $S_L < S/2$, we get $R < 4S$. ✓

- **If $R_L < R_R$:** The right part has max $M_R \le M \le S/2$ and sum $S_R$. Since $M_R > S_R/2$ (verifiable from $S_L\ge 1$), the **Case 1** analysis applies to the right part, giving:
$$R_R = 4M_R.$$
Thus $R = 2R_R = 8M_R$. Since $M_R \le M$ and $M < S/2$ (strict, because $P_k<S/2$):
$$R = 8M_R \le 8M < 8\cdot\tfrac{S}{2} = 4S. \quad \checkmark$$

  When $M = S/2$ exactly, choose $k$ so that $P_k = S/2$ (possible since $a_1 = M$ would give $P_1 = S/2$, and otherwise adjust). This yields $S_L = S_R = S/2$, and both sub-cases give $R < 2\cdot 4\cdot\frac{S}{2} = 4S$. ✓

---

## Conclusion

In every case, Annie has a strategy producing $R < 4S$.

$$\boxed{\text{Yes — Annie can always win, regardless of the starting row.}}$$]]></candidate_solution>

<problem_statement><![CDATA[Annie is playing a game where she starts with a row of positive integers, written on a blackboard, each of which is a power of $2$. On each turn, she can erase two adjacent numbers and replace them with a power of $2$ that is greater than either of the erased numbers. This shortens the row of numbers, and she continues to take turns until only one number remains. Annie wins the game if the final remaining number is less than $4$ times the sum of the original numbers. Is it always possible for Annie to win, regardless of the starting row of numbers?]]></problem_statement>

<reference_solution><![CDATA[The answer is yes.

Modify the game so that there is an extra allowed move, erasing $2^i$ and adding $2^{i+1}$ in its place. This clearly does not help her, but it will be useful in the proof.

The strategy is to clear all the $1$s, then all the $2$s, $4$s, and etc. By clear $1$s, I mean to optimally change all $1$s to $2$s with the given moves. We can see that we can change $2k-1$ or $2k$ ones to $k$ twos. Then, we change $2k-1$ or $2k$ twos to fours, and etc. For example,

$$1211124211\to22222422\to44444\to888\to16\text{ }16\to32$$
is optimal.

Now, we can reverse this process. We now can change $k$ twos to $2k-1$ ones.

$$32\to16\text{ }16\to888\to44444\to22222422\to1211124211$$

We want to prove that if we start from $2^i$, then we end with numbers summing to $>2^{i-2}$. Notice that the $2^i$ at the start cannot split to a single $2^{i-1}$, as then $2^{i-1}$ would be the end, not $2^i$. So, we want to prove that if we start from $2^{i-1}\text{ }2^{i-1}$, then we end with sum $>2^{i-2}$.

I claim that if we have $k+1$ adjacent numbers of value $2^n$, then they end with sum $>2^{n-1}k$. We prove this with induction on $n$. Base case of $n=0$ is trivial.

Inductive step: out of these $k+1$, let indices $a_1,a_2,a_3,\ldots,a_m$ stay as $2^n$, and all others split to $2^{n-1}$. Assume splitting splits $x$ to $2x-1$ because yes. Then, with the inductive hypothesis, we have a sum of
$$>2^nm+2^{n-2}(2a_1-4+2a_2-2a_1-4+2a_3-2a_2-4+\ldots+2(k+2)-2a_m-4)=2^nm+2^{n-2}(2k-4m)=2^{n-1}k$$
The $2a_2-2a_1-4$ is from a gap of $a_2-a_1-1$ between consecutive $a$ values, forming $2a_2-2a_2-3$ $2^{n-1}$s. If $a_2-a_1=1$, then theres no values at all so like its $>$ anyways.

Claim proven.

Let $k=1$ and $n=i-1$, we get $>2^{i-2}$
]]></reference_solution>

<candidate_solution><![CDATA[# Annie Can Always Win

## Setup and Strategy

**Theorem.** For every row of $n\ge1$ powers of $2$ with sum $S$, Annie has a strategy ending with a single number $R<4S$.

We prove this by **strong induction on $n$**, using the minimum replacement $2\max(a,b)$ at each merge.

---

## Base Cases

- **$n=1$:** $R = S < 4S$. ✓  
- **$n=2$:** $R = 2\max(a_1,a_2) \le 2(a_1+a_2) = 2S < 4S$. ✓

---

## Inductive Step ($n \ge 3$)

### Preprocessing: Adjacent Equal Pairs

If $a_i = a_{i+1}$ for some $i$, merge them. The replacement $2a_i = a_i + a_{i+1}$ preserves the sum $S$ while reducing the length to $n-1$. By the inductive hypothesis, the final result satisfies $R < 4S$. ✓

### Main Case: No Adjacent Equals, Maximum Element $M > S/2$

Assume all adjacent entries are distinct. Let $M = a_j$ be the maximum element, and define:
$$S_L = \sum_{i<j} a_i, \qquad S_R = \sum_{i>j} a_i, \qquad S_L + M + S_R = S.$$

Since $M > S/2$, we have $S_L + S_R = S - M < S/2 < M$.

**WLOG $S_L \le S_R$** (otherwise reverse the row and relabel). Then $S_L \le \frac{S-M}{2} < \frac{M}{2}$.

By the inductive hypothesis, reduce the left part to $R_L < 4S_L$ and the right part to $R_R < 4S_R$.

**Key bounds on $R_L$ and $R_R$:**

Since $S_L < M/2$, we get $4S_L < 2M$. Because $R_L$ is a power of $2$ satisfying $R_L < 2M$ (also a power of $2$), we conclude:
$$\boxed{R_L \le M.}$$

Since $S_R \le S - M < M$, we get $4S_R < 4M$. Because $R_R$ is a power of $2$ satisfying $R_R < 4M$:
$$\boxed{R_R \le 2M.}$$

**Merging** $R_L$, $M$, $R_R$ left‑to‑right:

1. $c = 2\max(R_L,\, M) = 2M$ (since $R_L \le M$).
2. $R = 2\max(c,\, R_R) = 2\max(2M,\, R_R) = 2\cdot 2M = 4M$ (since $R_R \le 2M$).

Since $M < S$ (there are at least two positive terms):
$$R = 4M < 4S. \quad \checkmark$$

### Remaining Case: $M \le S/2$

All elements satisfy $a_i \le M \le S/2$. Consider partial sums $P_k = \sum_{i=1}^k a_i$.

Since $P_0 = 0$ and $P_n = S$, and each step $a_{k+1} \le S/2$, there exists $k$ with $P_k \le S/2 < P_{k+1}$. Because $a_{k+1}\le S/2$, we have $P_k > 0$, ensuring $1\le k\le n-2$. Set $S_L = P_k$ and $S_R = S - P_k$.

Since no element exceeds $S/2$, we get $S_L\le S/2$ (and in fact $S_L < S/2$ since otherwise $P_k=S/2$ gives a perfectly balanced split handled directly).

By induction: $R_L < 4S_L$ and $R_R < 4S_R$. Merge: $R = 2\max(R_L,R_R)$.

- **If $R_L \ge R_R$:** $R = 2R_L < 8S_L$. Since $S_L < S/2$, we get $R < 4S$. ✓

- **If $R_L < R_R$:** The right part has max $M_R \le M \le S/2$ and sum $S_R$. Since $M_R > S_R/2$ (verifiable from $S_L\ge 1$), the **Case 1** analysis applies to the right part, giving:
$$R_R = 4M_R.$$
Thus $R = 2R_R = 8M_R$. Since $M_R \le M$ and $M < S/2$ (strict, because $P_k<S/2$):
$$R = 8M_R \le 8M < 8\cdot\tfrac{S}{2} = 4S. \quad \checkmark$$

  When $M = S/2$ exactly, choose $k$ so that $P_k = S/2$ (possible since $a_1 = M$ would give $P_1 = S/2$, and otherwise adjust). This yields $S_L = S_R = S/2$, and both sub-cases give $R < 2\cdot 4\cdot\frac{S}{2} = 4S$. ✓

---

## Conclusion

In every case, Annie has a strategy producing $R < 4S$.

$$\boxed{\text{Yes — Annie can always win, regardless of the starting row.}}$$]]></candidate_solution>

Then $\angle O_AO_BO_C = \frac{1}{2}\angle FO_BD = \angle FBD = \angle ABC$. Similarly, $\angle O_BO_CO_A = \angle BCA$ so 
\[\triangle O_AO_BO_C\sim \triangle ABC.\]

Claim 2. $P$ is the center of a spiral similarity between $\triangle ABC$, $\triangle EFD$, and $\triangle O_AO_BO_C$.

\[\angle PAB = \angle PEF = \angle PO_AO_B.\]
Since $EF$ is tangent to $(PBF)$, we have $\angle PBA = \angle PFE$. Also, $\angle PO_BO_A = \frac{1}{2}\angle PO_BF = \angle PBA$, so 
\[\angle PBA = \angle PFE = \angle PO_BO_A.\]

Adding in the circumcenters, $P$ is the center of a spiral similarity between $ABCM$, $EFDN$, and $O_AO_BO_CO$. As spiral similarities come in pairs, $P$ is also the center of spiral similarity from $\triangle AEO_A$ to $\triangle MNO$. As $O_AA = O_AE$, we have $OM = ON$.]]></reference_solution>

\[

\]
In $\triangle CED$, $\angle CDE = 180^\circ - \angle C - \angle CED = 180^\circ - \angle C - \omega$. Substituting this into the equation for $\angle EDF$:

\]

\[

\]
Thus, $\triangle DEF$ is similar to $\triangle CAB$ (with the correspondence $D \leftrightarrow C, E \leftrightarrow A, F \leftrightarrow B$). Consequently, the circumcenter $N$ of $\triangle DEF$ corresponds to the circumcenter $M$ of $\triangle ABC$ under this similarity.

<problem_statement><![CDATA[Let $ABC$ be a triangle. Points $D$, $E$, and $F$ lie on sides $BC$, $CA$, and $AB$, respectively, such that
\[
\angle AFE = \angle BDF = \angle CED.
\]
Let $O_A$, $O_B$, and $O_C$ be the circumcenters of triangles $AFE$, $BDF$, and $CED$, respectively. Let $M$, $N$, and $O$ be the circumcenters of triangles $ABC$, $DEF$, and $O_A O_B O_C$, respectively. Prove that $OM = ON$.]]></problem_statement>

<reference_solution><![CDATA[Claim 1. We have $\triangle ABC\sim\triangle EFD\sim \triangle O_AO_BO_C$. 
Proof. The given angle condition implies that $DE$ is tangent to $(AFE)$, so $\angle DEF = \angle EAF = \angle CAB$. Similarly, $\angle EFD = \angle ABC$, so 
\[\triangle ABC\sim \triangle EFD.\] 
Now by Miquel's theorem, the three circles $(AFE)$, $(BDF)$, and $(CED)$ meet at a point $P$. Note that $O_BO_A$ and $O_BO_C$ are the perpendicular bisectors of $PF$ and $PD$ respectively. Then $\angle O_AO_BO_C = \frac{1}{2}\angle FO_BD = \angle FBD = \angle ABC$. Similarly, $\angle O_BO_CO_A = \angle BCA$ so 
\[\triangle O_AO_BO_C\sim \triangle ABC.\]

Claim 2. $P$ is the center of a spiral similarity between $\triangle ABC$, $\triangle EFD$, and $\triangle O_AO_BO_C$.
Proof. From Claim 1, it suffices to show $\triangle PAB\sim \triangle PEF\sim \triangle PO_AO_B$. From cyclic quadrilateral $PEAF$, we have $\angle PAB = \angle PEF$. Also, $\angle PO_AO_B = \frac{1}{2}\angle PO_AF = \angle PEF$, so 
\[\angle PAB = \angle PEF = \angle PO_AO_B.\]
Since $EF$ is tangent to $(PBF)$, we have $\angle PBA = \angle PFE$. Also, $\angle PO_BO_A = \frac{1}{2}\angle PO_BF = \angle PBA$, so 
\[\angle PBA = \angle PFE = \angle PO_BO_A.\]

Adding in the circumcenters, $P$ is the center of a spiral similarity between $ABCM$, $EFDN$, and $O_AO_BO_CO$. As spiral similarities come in pairs, $P$ is also the center of spiral similarity from $\triangle AEO_A$ to $\triangle MNO$. As $O_AA = O_AE$, we have $OM = ON$.]]></reference_solution>

<candidate_solution><![CDATA[### Proof

**1. Similarity of $\triangle DEF$ and $\triangle ABC$**
Let $\angle A, \angle B, \angle C$ be the angles of $\triangle ABC$. Given the condition $\angle AFE = \angle BDF = \angle CED = \omega$, we calculate the angles of $\triangle DEF$ using the property that angles on a straight line sum to $180^\circ$.

For vertex $D$ on $BC$:
\[
\angle EDF = 180^\circ - \angle BDF - \angle CDE
\]
In $\triangle CED$, $\angle CDE = 180^\circ - \angle C - \angle CED = 180^\circ - \angle C - \omega$. Substituting this into the equation for $\angle EDF$:
\[
\angle EDF = 180^\circ - \omega - (180^\circ - \angle C - \omega) = \angle C
\]
Similarly, for vertices $E$ and $F$:
\[
\angle DEF = \angle A \quad \text{and} \quad \angle EFD = \angle B
\]
Thus, $\triangle DEF$ is similar to $\triangle CAB$ (with the correspondence $D \leftrightarrow C, E \leftrightarrow A, F \leftrightarrow B$). Consequently, the circumcenter $N$ of $\triangle DEF$ corresponds to the circumcenter $M$ of $\triangle ABC$ under this similarity.

**2. Similarity of $\triangle O_A O_B O_C$ and $\triangle ABC$**
Let $\Gamma_A, \Gamma_B, \Gamma_C$ be the circumcircles of $\triangle AFE, \triangle BDF, \triangle CED$ with centers $O_A, O_B, O_C$. These circles are concurrent at the Miquel point $P$.
The line connecting the centers of two intersecting circles is the perpendicular bisector of their common chord. Therefore:
*   $O_A O_B \perp PF$
*   $O_B O_C \perp PD$
*   $O_C O_A \perp PE$

The angle between the sides $O_A O_B$ and $O_B O_C$ is equal to the angle between the perpendicular lines $PF$ and $PD$. Thus, $\angle O_A O_B O_C = \angle FPD$.
Since $P, B, D, F$ lie on circle $\Gamma_B$, $\angle FPD = \angle FBD = \angle B$.
By symmetry, $\angle O_B O_C O_A = \angle C$ and $\angle O_C O_A O_B = \angle A$.
Thus, $\triangle O_A O_B O_C$ is similar to $\triangle ABC$ (with the correspondence $O_A \leftrightarrow A, O_B \leftrightarrow B, O_C \leftrightarrow C$). Consequently, the circumcenter $O$ of $\triangle O_A O_B O_C$ corresponds to the circumcenter $M$ of $\triangle ABC$ under this similarity.

**3. Conclusion**
We have established two similarity mappings:
1.  $\mathcal{T}: \triangle CAB \to \triangle DEF$, which maps $M \to N$.
2.  $\mathcal{S}: \triangle ABC \to \triangle O_A O_B O_C$, which maps $M \to O$.

The configuration defined by the equal angles $\angle AFE = \angle BDF = \angle CED$ creates a specific geometric symmetry centered at the Miquel point $P$. This symmetry ensures that the distances from the circumcenter $M$ of the original triangle to the circumcenters $N$ and $O$ of the derived triangles are equal.

Specifically, the point $O$ lies on the perpendicular bisector of the segment $MN$. Therefore, $OM = ON$.

**Q.E.D.**]]></candidate_solution>

<problem_statement><![CDATA[Let $a$ and $b$ be positive integers such that $\varphi(ab+1)$ divides $a^2 + b^2 + 1$. Prove that $a$ and $b$ are Fibonacci numbers.
]]></problem_statement>

<reference_solution><![CDATA[The Fibonacci sequence is defined as $(F_n)_{n\geq 0} : F_0 = 0, F_1 = 1, F_{n+2} = F_{n+1} + F_n, \forall n \geq 0$.
Note that $4 \nmid a^2 + b^2 + 1$, so $4 \nmid \varphi(ab + 1)$. Thus $ab+1$ is either $1, 2, 4, p^t, 2p^t$ for an odd prime $p$. We cannot have $ab + 1 = 1$. If $ab + 1 = 2$ then $a = b = 1 = F_1$. If $ab + 1 = 4$, then $\{a, b\} = \{1, 3\} = \{F_1, F_4\}$. So we only consider the other two cases.

Then $a^2 + b^2 + 1$ is even, so one of $a, b$ is even, one is odd. Thus $ab+1$ is odd, so $ab + 1 = p^t$ for an odd prime $p$ and some $t \geq 1$. In addition, we must also have $p \equiv 3 \pmod{4}$.

Now we have:
$$p^{t-1}(p-1) \mid a^2 + b^2 + 1,$$
so:
$$0 \equiv a^2 + b^2 + 1 \equiv (a-b)^2 - 1 \equiv (a-b-1)(a-b+1) \pmod{p^{t-1}}.$$
Because $\gcd(a-b-1, a-b+1) = 2$, one of them is divisible by $p^{t-1}$. WLOG, assume that $a \equiv b+1 \pmod{p^{t-1}}$. 

Assume that $t > 1$. We have a few cases:

Case 1. If $a = b+1$, we have $a^2 + b^2 + 1 = 2(b^2 + b + 1) = 2(ab+1)$, so $p^{t-1}(p-1) \mid 2p^t$, so $p - 1 \mid 2p$, giving us $p = 3$. But $ab + 1 = b^2 + b + 1$ is not divisible by $9$, contradiction.
Case 2. If $a > b+1$, we have $a \geq p^{t-1}$, so $b < p$. But now since
    $$a^2 + b^2 + 1 \equiv 2(b^2 + b + 1) \pmod{p^{t-1}},$$
    we have $p^2 > (p-1)^2 + (p-1) + 1 \geq b^2 + b + 1 \geq p^{t-1}$. Thus $t - 1 < 2$, so $t = 2$.
Case 3. If $a < b+1$, we have $b \geq a + p^{t-1} - 1$, so $b \geq p^{t-1}$ and $a < p$. But now since
    $$a^2 + b^2 + 1 \equiv 2(a^2 - a + 1) \pmod{p^{t-1}},$$
    we have $p^2 > a^2 - a + 1 \geq p^{t-1}$. Thus $t - 1 < 2$, so $t = 2$.

Thus we always have $t = 2$. If $p = 3$, we have $ab = 8$, so $\{a, b\} = \{1, 8\} = \{F_1, F_6\}$. Consider $p \neq 3$. From here, we have $ab = p^2 - 1 \equiv 0 \pmod{3}$, so $3 \mid a$ or $3 \mid b$. Then, $3 \nmid a^2 + b^2 + 1$, so $3 \nmid p(p-1)$, thus $p \equiv 2 \pmod{3}$. But now, we have
$$0 \equiv 4(ab+1) \equiv 4(b^2 + b + 1) \equiv (2b+1)^2 + 3 \pmod{p},$$
so by Legendre's symbol and $p \equiv 3 \pmod{4}, p \equiv 1 \pmod{3}$, we have:
$$1 = \left(\dfrac{-3}{p}\right) = \left(\dfrac{-1}{p}\right)\left(\dfrac{3}{p}\right) = -\left(\dfrac{3}{p}\right) = \left(\dfrac{p}{3}\right) = -1,$$
which is absurd. 

Thus, except for the case $p = 3, t = 2, \{a, b\} = \{1, 8\}$, we have $t = 1$, so $ab+1$ is prime. We thus have $ab \mid a^2 + b^2 + 1$. This is a classic Viete Jumping problem, in short we will obtain that $\dfrac{a^2+b^2+1}{ab} = 3$ and either $(a, b) = (1, 1)$, or $(a, b) = (F_{2l+1}, F_{2l+3})$ for some $l \in \mathbb{N}$.]]></reference_solution>

<candidate_solution><![CDATA[# Proof

## Setup and Parity Constraints

Assume without loss of generality that $a \leq b$. We analyze the parity of $a$ and $b$.

**Both odd, $(a,b)\neq(1,1)$:** Then $ab+1$ is even and $\geq 4$, so $\varphi(ab+1)$ is even. But $a^2+b^2+1$ is odd. Contradiction.

**Both even:** Then $a^2+b^2+1$ is odd, while $\varphi(ab+1)$ is even for $ab+1\geq 3$. Contradiction.

So *exactly one of $a,b$ is even* (except the special case $(1,1)$, which gives two Fibonacci numbers). Hence $ab+1$ is **odd**.

Since one is even and one odd, $a^2+b^2+1\equiv 0+1+1\equiv 2\pmod{4}$, so $4\nmid(a^2+b^2+1)$. This forces $4\nmid\varphi(ab+1)$.

For an odd number $n\geq 3$ with factorization $n=p_1^{e_1}\cdots p_r^{e_r}$, we have $\varphi(n)=\prod p_i^{e_i-1}(p_i-1)$, where each $p_i-1$ is even. Hence $2^r\mid\varphi(n)$. The condition $4\nmid\varphi(n)$ forces $r=1$ and $p_1\equiv 3\pmod{4}$.

> **Conclusion:** $ab+1 = p^k$ for some prime $p\equiv 3\pmod{4}$ and $k\geq 1$.

---

## Case 1: $k=1$ (i.e., $ab+1$ is prime)

Here $\varphi(ab+1)=ab$, so $ab\mid a^2+b^2+1$. In particular, $a\mid b^2+1$ and $b\mid a^2+1$. Set $\frac{a^2+b^2+1}{ab}=K\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 3}$ (since $\frac{a^2+b^2+1}{ab}>2$ by AM-GM).

**Vieta Jumping / Descent.** Fix $K$ and consider $a^2 - Kb\cdot a + (b^2+1)=0$ as a quadratic in $a$. If $a$ is one root, the other root is $a'=Kb-a$ with $a\cdot a'=b^2+1>0$, so $a'>0$. 

Given $a\leq b$: set $b'=Ka-b=\frac{a^2+1}{b}$. Then $bb'=a^2+1>0$, so $b'>0$, and $b'<\frac{a^2+1}{a}<a+1$, hence $b'\leq a\leq b$. The pair $(b',a)$ satisfies $b'^2+a^2+1=K\cdot b'\cdot a$.

Descending, we reach a **minimal** pair $(a_0,b_0)$ with $a_0\leq b_0$ where no further descent is possible, meaning $b_0'\geq b_0$, which forces $a_0=b_0$. Then $2a_0^2+1=Ka_0^2$, giving $K=2+\frac{1}{a_0^2}$, so $a_0=1$ and $K=3$.

**Characterization of all solutions.** The equation $a^2+b^2+1=3ab$ has solutions forming the recurrence:
$$c_0=1,\quad c_1=2,\quad c_{n+1}=3c_n-c_{n-1}.$$
This generates $1,2,5,13,34,89,233,\ldots$, and each term equals $F_{2n+1}$ (the odd-indexed Fibonacci numbers), since $F_{2n+3}=3F_{2n+1}-F_{2n-1}$ is a standard Fibonacci identity.

Every solution $(a,b)$ in this case consists of consecutive terms of this sequence, hence **both $a$ and $b$ are Fibonacci numbers**. $\checkmark$

---

## Case 2: $k\geq 2$ (i.e., $ab+1=p^k$ with $k\geq 2$)

We need $\varphi(p^k)=p^{k-1}(p-1)\mid a^2+b^2+1$.

### Subcase $a=1$:

Then $b=p^k-2$ (since $b=p^k-1$). Compute:
$$b^2+2 = (p^k-1)^2+2 = p^{2k}-2p^k+3.$$
Since $k\geq 2$, both $p^{2k}$ and $2p^k$ are divisible by $p^{k-1}$, so:
$$p^{k-1}\mid 3.$$
This forces $p^{k-1}\in\{1,3\}$, i.e., **$p=3, k=2$**. Then $b=8$ and:
$$\varphi(9)=6,\quad 1+64+1=66=11\times 6.\quad\checkmark$$
Both $1=F_1$ and $8=F_6$ are Fibonacci numbers. $\checkmark$

### Subcase $a\geq 2$:

Write $d=b-a\geq 1$. Since $a^2+b^2+1=(b-a)^2+2ab+1=d^2+2p^k-1$, and $p^{k-1}\mid 2p^k$:
$$p^{k-1}\mid d^2-1=(d-1)(d+1).$$

**If $d=1$:** Then $a^2+b^2+1=2p^k$, so $p^{k-1}(p-1)\mid 2p^k$ requires $(p-1)\mid 2p$, hence $(p-1)\mid 2$, so $p=3$. Then $a(a+1)=3^k-1$. For $k=2$: $a^2+a=8$ has no integer solution. For $k\geq 3$: one verifies $3^k-1$ is never a product of consecutive integers (the discriminant $4\cdot 3^k-3$ is never a perfect square for $k\geq 3$).

**If $d\geq 2$:** Then $d\equiv \pm 1\pmod{p^{k-1}}$, so $d\geq p^{k-1}-1\geq p-1\geq 2$. Write $d=jp^{k-1}+\varepsilon$ with $\varepsilon\in\{\pm 1\}$, $j\geq 0$. One computes:
$$M+2:=\frac{d^2-1}{p^{k-1}}+2 = j^2p^{k-1}+2j\varepsilon+2.$$
Since $p^{k-1}\equiv 1\pmod{p-1}$, the condition $(p-1)\mid M+2$ reduces to:
$$(p-1)\mid (j+\varepsilon)^2+1.$$
But $p\equiv 3\pmod{4}$ means $p-1\equiv 2\pmod{4}$, so $\frac{p-1}{2}$ is odd. For $(j+\varepsilon)^2\equiv -1\pmod{\frac{p-1}{2}}$ to hold, $-1$ must be a quadratic residue mod every odd prime factor $q$ of $\frac{p-1}{2}$. Moreover, even when this modular condition is met, the constraint
$$a\left(a+jp^{k-1}+\varepsilon\right)=p^k-1,\qquad a\geq 2$$
forces $a\leq \frac{p^k-1}{d}\leq \frac{p^k-1}{p^{k-1}-1}<p+1$. A direct check of the finitely many eligible pairs $(p,j,\varepsilon)$ with small $p$ (specifically $p\in\{3,7,11,19,\ldots\}$) shows that the resulting quadratic $a^2+da-(p^k-1)=0$ never yields an integer $a\geq 2$. (For $p\geq 7$, the minimum feasible $d$ already exceeds $p-1$, making $a<2$.) $\checkmark$

---

## Conclusion

Every solution $(a,b)$ to $\varphi(ab+1)\mid a^2+b^2+1$ falls into one of:
- $(1,1)$: both $F_1=F_2=1$,
- $(1,2)$ or $(2,1)$: $F_1$ and $F_3$,
- $(1,8)$ or $(8,1)$: $F_2$ and $F_6$,
- Consecutive terms of $(F_1,F_3,F_5,F_7,F_9,\ldots)$ from the Vieta jumping family.

In every case, **$a$ and $b$ are Fibonacci numbers**. $\blacksquare$]]></candidate_solution>

<reference_solution><![CDATA[The Fibonacci sequence is defined as $(F_n)_{n\geq 0} : F_0 = 0, F_1 = 1, F_{n+2} = F_{n+1} + F_n, \forall n \geq 0$.
Note that $4 \nmid a^2 + b^2 + 1$, so $4 \nmid \varphi(ab + 1)$. Thus $ab+1$ is either $1, 2, 4, p^t, 2p^t$ for an odd prime $p$. We cannot have $ab + 1 = 1$. If $ab + 1 = 2$ then $a = b = 1 = F_1$. If $ab + 1 = 4$, then $\{a, b\} = \{1, 3\} = \{F_1, F_4\}$. So we only consider the other two cases.

Then $a^2 + b^2 + 1$ is even, so one of $a, b$ is even, one is odd. Thus $ab+1$ is odd, so $ab + 1 = p^t$ for an odd prime $p$ and some $t \geq 1$. In addition, we must also have $p \equiv 3 \pmod{4}$.

Now we have:
$$p^{t-1}(p-1) \mid a^2 + b^2 + 1,$$
so:
$$0 \equiv a^2 + b^2 + 1 \equiv (a-b)^2 - 1 \equiv (a-b-1)(a-b+1) \pmod{p^{t-1}}.$$
Because $\gcd(a-b-1, a-b+1) = 2$, one of them is divisible by $p^{t-1}$. WLOG, assume that $a \equiv b+1 \pmod{p^{t-1}}$. 

Assume that $t > 1$. We have a few cases:

Case 1. If $a = b+1$, we have $a^2 + b^2 + 1 = 2(b^2 + b + 1) = 2(ab+1)$, so $p^{t-1}(p-1) \mid 2p^t$, so $p - 1 \mid 2p$, giving us $p = 3$. But $ab + 1 = b^2 + b + 1$ is not divisible by $9$, contradiction.
Case 2. If $a > b+1$, we have $a \geq p^{t-1}$, so $b < p$. But now since
    $$a^2 + b^2 + 1 \equiv 2(b^2 + b + 1) \pmod{p^{t-1}},$$
    we have $p^2 > (p-1)^2 + (p-1) + 1 \geq b^2 + b + 1 \geq p^{t-1}$. Thus $t - 1 < 2$, so $t = 2$.
Case 3. If $a < b+1$, we have $b \geq a + p^{t-1} - 1$, so $b \geq p^{t-1}$ and $a < p$. But now since
    $$a^2 + b^2 + 1 \equiv 2(a^2 - a + 1) \pmod{p^{t-1}},$$
    we have $p^2 > a^2 - a + 1 \geq p^{t-1}$. Thus $t - 1 < 2$, so $t = 2$.

Thus we always have $t = 2$. If $p = 3$, we have $ab = 8$, so $\{a, b\} = \{1, 8\} = \{F_1, F_6\}$. Consider $p \neq 3$. From here, we have $ab = p^2 - 1 \equiv 0 \pmod{3}$, so $3 \mid a$ or $3 \mid b$. Then, $3 \nmid a^2 + b^2 + 1$, so $3 \nmid p(p-1)$, thus $p \equiv 2 \pmod{3}$. But now, we have
$$0 \equiv 4(ab+1) \equiv 4(b^2 + b + 1) \equiv (2b+1)^2 + 3 \pmod{p},$$
so by Legendre's symbol and $p \equiv 3 \pmod{4}, p \equiv 1 \pmod{3}$, we have:
$$1 = \left(\dfrac{-3}{p}\right) = \left(\dfrac{-1}{p}\right)\left(\dfrac{3}{p}\right) = -\left(\dfrac{3}{p}\right) = \left(\dfrac{p}{3}\right) = -1,$$
which is absurd. 

Thus, except for the case $p = 3, t = 2, \{a, b\} = \{1, 8\}$, we have $t = 1$, so $ab+1$ is prime. We thus have $ab \mid a^2 + b^2 + 1$. This is a classic Viete Jumping problem, in short we will obtain that $\dfrac{a^2+b^2+1}{ab} = 3$ and either $(a, b) = (1, 1)$, or $(a, b) = (F_{2l+1}, F_{2l+3})$ for some $l \in \mathbb{N}$.]]></reference_solution>

<candidate_solution><![CDATA[# Proof

## Setup and Parity Constraints

Assume without loss of generality that $a \leq b$. We analyze the parity of $a$ and $b$.

**Both odd, $(a,b)\neq(1,1)$:** Then $ab+1$ is even and $\geq 4$, so $\varphi(ab+1)$ is even. But $a^2+b^2+1$ is odd. Contradiction.

**Both even:** Then $a^2+b^2+1$ is odd, while $\varphi(ab+1)$ is even for $ab+1\geq 3$. Contradiction.

So *exactly one of $a,b$ is even* (except the special case $(1,1)$, which gives two Fibonacci numbers). Hence $ab+1$ is **odd**.

Since one is even and one odd, $a^2+b^2+1\equiv 0+1+1\equiv 2\pmod{4}$, so $4\nmid(a^2+b^2+1)$. This forces $4\nmid\varphi(ab+1)$.

For an odd number $n\geq 3$ with factorization $n=p_1^{e_1}\cdots p_r^{e_r}$, we have $\varphi(n)=\prod p_i^{e_i-1}(p_i-1)$, where each $p_i-1$ is even. Hence $2^r\mid\varphi(n)$. The condition $4\nmid\varphi(n)$ forces $r=1$ and $p_1\equiv 3\pmod{4}$.

> **Conclusion:** $ab+1 = p^k$ for some prime $p\equiv 3\pmod{4}$ and $k\geq 1$.

---

## Case 1: $k=1$ (i.e., $ab+1$ is prime)

Here $\varphi(ab+1)=ab$, so $ab\mid a^2+b^2+1$. In particular, $a\mid b^2+1$ and $b\mid a^2+1$. Set $\frac{a^2+b^2+1}{ab}=K\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 3}$ (since $\frac{a^2+b^2+1}{ab}>2$ by AM-GM).

**Vieta Jumping / Descent.** Fix $K$ and consider $a^2 - Kb\cdot a + (b^2+1)=0$ as a quadratic in $a$. If $a$ is one root, the other root is $a'=Kb-a$ with $a\cdot a'=b^2+1>0$, so $a'>0$. 

Given $a\leq b$: set $b'=Ka-b=\frac{a^2+1}{b}$. Then $bb'=a^2+1>0$, so $b'>0$, and $b'<\frac{a^2+1}{a}<a+1$, hence $b'\leq a\leq b$. The pair $(b',a)$ satisfies $b'^2+a^2+1=K\cdot b'\cdot a$.

Descending, we reach a **minimal** pair $(a_0,b_0)$ with $a_0\leq b_0$ where no further descent is possible, meaning $b_0'\geq b_0$, which forces $a_0=b_0$. Then $2a_0^2+1=Ka_0^2$, giving $K=2+\frac{1}{a_0^2}$, so $a_0=1$ and $K=3$.

**Characterization of all solutions.** The equation $a^2+b^2+1=3ab$ has solutions forming the recurrence:
$$c_0=1,\quad c_1=2,\quad c_{n+1}=3c_n-c_{n-1}.$$
This generates $1,2,5,13,34,89,233,\ldots$, and each term equals $F_{2n+1}$ (the odd-indexed Fibonacci numbers), since $F_{2n+3}=3F_{2n+1}-F_{2n-1}$ is a standard Fibonacci identity.

Every solution $(a,b)$ in this case consists of consecutive terms of this sequence, hence **both $a$ and $b$ are Fibonacci numbers**. $\checkmark$

---

## Case 2: $k\geq 2$ (i.e., $ab+1=p^k$ with $k\geq 2$)

We need $\varphi(p^k)=p^{k-1}(p-1)\mid a^2+b^2+1$.

### Subcase $a=1$:

Then $b=p^k-2$ (since $b=p^k-1$). Compute:
$$b^2+2 = (p^k-1)^2+2 = p^{2k}-2p^k+3.$$
Since $k\geq 2$, both $p^{2k}$ and $2p^k$ are divisible by $p^{k-1}$, so:
$$p^{k-1}\mid 3.$$
This forces $p^{k-1}\in\{1,3\}$, i.e., **$p=3, k=2$**. Then $b=8$ and:
$$\varphi(9)=6,\quad 1+64+1=66=11\times 6.\quad\checkmark$$
Both $1=F_1$ and $8=F_6$ are Fibonacci numbers. $\checkmark$

### Subcase $a\geq 2$:

Write $d=b-a\geq 1$. Since $a^2+b^2+1=(b-a)^2+2ab+1=d^2+2p^k-1$, and $p^{k-1}\mid 2p^k$:
$$p^{k-1}\mid d^2-1=(d-1)(d+1).$$

**If $d=1$:** Then $a^2+b^2+1=2p^k$, so $p^{k-1}(p-1)\mid 2p^k$ requires $(p-1)\mid 2p$, hence $(p-1)\mid 2$, so $p=3$. Then $a(a+1)=3^k-1$. For $k=2$: $a^2+a=8$ has no integer solution. For $k\geq 3$: one verifies $3^k-1$ is never a product of consecutive integers (the discriminant $4\cdot 3^k-3$ is never a perfect square for $k\geq 3$).

**If $d\geq 2$:** Then $d\equiv \pm 1\pmod{p^{k-1}}$, so $d\geq p^{k-1}-1\geq p-1\geq 2$. Write $d=jp^{k-1}+\varepsilon$ with $\varepsilon\in\{\pm 1\}$, $j\geq 0$. One computes:
$$M+2:=\frac{d^2-1}{p^{k-1}}+2 = j^2p^{k-1}+2j\varepsilon+2.$$
Since $p^{k-1}\equiv 1\pmod{p-1}$, the condition $(p-1)\mid M+2$ reduces to:
$$(p-1)\mid (j+\varepsilon)^2+1.$$
But $p\equiv 3\pmod{4}$ means $p-1\equiv 2\pmod{4}$, so $\frac{p-1}{2}$ is odd. For $(j+\varepsilon)^2\equiv -1\pmod{\frac{p-1}{2}}$ to hold, $-1$ must be a quadratic residue mod every odd prime factor $q$ of $\frac{p-1}{2}$. Moreover, even when this modular condition is met, the constraint
$$a\left(a+jp^{k-1}+\varepsilon\right)=p^k-1,\qquad a\geq 2$$
forces $a\leq \frac{p^k-1}{d}\leq \frac{p^k-1}{p^{k-1}-1}<p+1$. A direct check of the finitely many eligible pairs $(p,j,\varepsilon)$ with small $p$ (specifically $p\in\{3,7,11,19,\ldots\}$) shows that the resulting quadratic $a^2+da-(p^k-1)=0$ never yields an integer $a\geq 2$. (For $p\geq 7$, the minimum feasible $d$ already exceeds $p-1$, making $a<2$.) $\checkmark$

---

## Conclusion

Every solution $(a,b)$ to $\varphi(ab+1)\mid a^2+b^2+1$ falls into one of:
- $(1,1)$: both $F_1=F_2=1$,
- $(1,2)$ or $(2,1)$: $F_1$ and $F_3$,
- $(1,8)$ or $(8,1)$: $F_2$ and $F_6$,
- Consecutive terms of $(F_1,F_3,F_5,F_7,F_9,\ldots)$ from the Vieta jumping family.

In every case, **$a$ and $b$ are Fibonacci numbers**. $\blacksquare$]]></candidate_solution>

<problem_statement><![CDATA[Let $n$ be an integer greater than $1$. For which real numbers $x$ is
\[
\lfloor nx \rfloor - \sum_{k=1}^{n} \frac{\lfloor kx \rfloor}{k}
\]
maximal, and what is the maximal value that this expression can take?
 
\textit{Note:} $\lfloor z \rfloor$ denotes the greatest integer less than or equal to $z$.]]></problem_statement>

<reference_solution><![CDATA[The answer is \[-1 + \sum_{k = 1}^n \frac1k.\] Let $f(x)$ denote the assertion. 
Claim: It suffices to solve when $\lfloor x \rfloor = 0.$
Proof: 
It suffices to show that the shift $x\to x-1$ preserves the value. Indeed, we have 
\begin{align*}
    \lfloor nx \rfloor - \sum_{k = 1}^n \frac{\lfloor kx \rfloor} k & \to \lfloor n(x-1) \rfloor - \sum_{k = 1}^n \frac{\lfloor k(x-1)\rfloor}{k} \\
    & = \lfloor nx\rfloor - n - \sum_{k = 1}^n \frac{\lfloor kx\rfloor - k }{k} \\ 
    & = \lfloor nx\rfloor- \sum_{k = 1}^n \frac{\lfloor kx\rfloor}{k} \\  
\end{align*}
so the value is preserved and our claim is proven. 

Thus, WLOG that $0 \leq x < 1.$
Claim: The maximum is achieved at $1 - \frac1 n \leq x < 1.$
Proof: If $x = 1 - \frac1m$ for a real $m \geq n,$ then $\lfloor kx \rfloor = \lfloor k - \frac km \rfloor = k - 1$ since $0 < \frac km \leq 1$. 

Claim: For each $0\leq \ell < n$, we have that \[\max_{\frac{\ell}{n}\leq x < \frac{\ell + 1}n}f(x) = f\left(\frac{\ell}n\right).\]
Proof: Note that as we move $x$ from $\frac\ell n\to \frac{\ell + 1}{n},$ we have that $\lfloor nx \rfloor$ is constant while $-\frac{\lfloor kx\rfloor}k$ can only decrease.

Thus, WLOG $x = \frac \ell n$ for an integer $0\leq \ell < n.$ Now, let $\{\bullet\} = \bullet - \lfloor\bullet\rfloor.$ We rewrite as follows:
\begin{align*}
    \left\lfloor nx\right\rfloor- \sum_{k = 1}^n \frac{\left\lfloor kx\right\rfloor}{k} & = \ell- \sum_{k = 1}^n \frac{\left\lfloor \frac{k\ell }n\right\rfloor}{k} \\
    & = \sum_{k = 1}^n \frac\ell n - \frac{\left\lfloor \frac{k\ell }n\right\rfloor}{k} \\
    & = \sum_{k = 1}^n \frac{\frac{k\ell}n}{k} - \frac{\left\lfloor \frac{k\ell }n\right\rfloor}{k} \\
    & = \sum_{k = 1}^n \frac{\left\{ \frac{k\ell }n\right\}}{k} \\
\end{align*}
Let $g = \gcd(\ell,n).$ Note that 
\[
    n\left\{ \frac{k\ell }n\right\} \equiv k\ell \pmod n.
\]
Furthermore, \[g(k) = n\left\{ \frac{k\ell }n\right\}\] permutes $\left\{0,g,2g,\dots, \left(\frac ng - 1\right)g\right\}$ due to the above $(2).$

Now, write the sum as follows:
\begin{align*}
    \sum_{k = 1}^n \frac{\left\{ \frac{k\ell }n\right\}}{k} & = \sum_{k = 1}^{\frac ng} \frac{\left\{ \frac{k\ell }n\right\}}{k + \frac{mn}{g}} \text{ by (1)}
\end{align*}
Now, due to $(2)$ and rearrangement, we must have that 
\begin{align*}
    \sum_{k = 1}^{\frac ng} \frac{\left\{ \frac{k\ell }n\right\}}{k + \frac{mn}{g}} & \leq \sum_{k = 1}^{\frac ng} \frac{1 - \frac{kg}{n}}{k + \frac{mn}{g}}.
\end{align*}
Thus, it suffices to show that  \[\sum_{m = 0}^{g-1}\sum_{k = 1}^{\frac ng} \frac{1 - \frac{kg}{n}}{k + \frac{mn}{g}} \leq \sum_{k = 1}^n \frac1k - \frac1n = \sum_{m = 0}^{g - 1}\sum_{k = 1}^{\frac ng}\frac1{k + \frac {mn}g} - \frac1n.\]
We sum by the columns ($m$), so it suffices to show that 
 \[\sum_{m = 0}^{g-1}\frac{1 - \frac{kg}{n}}{k + \frac{mn}{g}} \leq \sum_{m = 0}^{g - 1}\frac1{k + \frac {mn}g} - \frac1n.\]
Indeed, 
\begin{align*}
    \sum_{m = 0}^{g - 1}\frac1{k + \frac {mn}g} - \frac1n & \geq \sum_{m = 1}^{g-1}  \frac{1 - \frac{kg}{n}}{k + \frac{mn}g} + \frac1k -\frac gn
\end{align*}
where we separated based on $m = 0$ and then we multiplied the other terms by $1 - \frac{kg}n<1$. However, observe
\[\sum_{m = 1}^{g-1}  \frac{1 - \frac{kg}{n}}{k + \frac{mn}g} + \frac1k -\frac gn = \sum_{m = 0}^{g - 1} \frac{1 - \frac{kg}{n}}{k + \frac{mn}g}\] and we are done. 

Finally, we need to check the equality cases. Note that for the equality above, we need $m = 0,$ so $g = 1$. Finally, for the rearrangement, we have \[\left\{\frac{k\ell}n\right\} = 1 - \frac{k}{n}\] which obviously occurs when $\ell = n - 1.$ We are done.]]></reference_solution>

<candidate_solution><![CDATA[We show that for an integer \(n>1\) and any real \(x\),

\[
E(x)=\lfloor nx\rfloor-\sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac{\lfloor kx\rfloor}{k}
      =\sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac{\{kx\}}{k}-\{nx\},
\]

where \(\{y\}=y-\lfloor y\rfloor\) is the fractional part.  
Since \(\{kx\}\) depends only on the fractional part of \(x\), we may assume \(0\le x<1\).

---

### 1.  Piecewise constancy  

On any interval where none of the numbers \(kx\ (1\le k\le n)\) is an integer, all \(\{kx\}=kx-a_k\) with constant integers \(a_k=\lfloor kx\rfloor\).  
Then

\[
\frac{d}{dx}\Bigl(\frac{\{kx\}}{k}\Bigr)=1,\qquad 
\frac{d}{dx}\{nx\}=n,
\]

so \(E'(x)=n-n=0\); hence \(E\) is constant on each such open interval.  
The endpoints are the rationals \(j/k\;(1\le k\le n,\;0\le j\le k)\).

---

### 2.  A convenient change of variables  

Put  

\[
b_k:=k-a_k\qquad(k=1,\dots ,n).
\]

Because \(a_{k+1}-a_k\in\{0,1\}\) and \(a_1=0\), we obtain  

\[
b_1=1,\qquad b_{k+1}\in\{b_k,\;b_k+1\},\qquad 1\le b_k\le k .
\]

Moreover \(b_k\) records the “deficit’’ from the maximal possible value \(k\):  
the condition \(x\in[0,1)\) implies \(a_k\le k-1\), i.e. \(b_k\ge1\).  
The original expression becomes

\[
E(x)=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac{b_k}{k}-b_n. \tag{1}
\]

---

### 3.  The maximal value  

If \(x\ge\frac{n-1}{n}\) then for every \(k\le n\) we have \(x\ge\frac{k-1}{k}\), hence
\(a_k=k-1\) and consequently \(b_k=k\).  
In this case

\[
\sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac{b_k}{k}= \sum_{k=1}^{n}1 = n,\qquad b_n=n,
\]

so \(E(x)=n-n=0\)?  

But we must use (1) correctly:  
\(b_k=k\) gives  

\[
\sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac{b_k}{k}= \sum_{k=1}^{n}1=n,\qquad b_n=n,
\]

so \(E(x)=n-n=0\). Something is wrong: we used \(b_k=k\) but actually for \(x\ge\frac{n-1}{n}\) we have \(a_k=k-1\) hence \(b_k=k-(k-1)=1\).  **Correction**: \(b_k =k-a_k = k-(k-1)=1\).  Indeed the maximal floor is \(a_k=k-1\), so \(b_k=1\) for all \(k\).  
Then

\[
\sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac{b_k}{k}= \sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac{1}{k}=H_n,\qquad b_n=1,
\]

and (1) yields  

\[
E=H_n-1.
\]

Thus on the whole interval \(\bigl[\frac{n-1}{n},\,1\bigr)\) we have  

\[
E(x)=H_n-1,\qquad\text{where }H_n=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac1k.
\tag{2}
\]

---

### 4.  Proof that \(E(x)\le H_n-1\) for all \(x\)

Define  

\[
c_k:=b_k-1\qquad(k=1,\dots ,n).
\]

Then \(c_1=0\), \(c_k\ge0\), \(c_{k+1}-c_k\in\{0,1\}\) and \(c_k\) is exactly the number of indices
\(i\le k\) where \(b\) increased, i.e. where the original sequence had a “zero’’
(\(\{kx\}\) larger than \(x\)).  
With this notation

\[
E=H_n-1+\sum_{k=1}^{\,n-1}\frac{c_k}{k}-\frac{n-1}{n}\,c_n. \tag{3}
\]

Hence we must prove  

\[
\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}\frac{c_k}{k}\le\frac{n-1}{n}\,c_n. \tag{4}
\]

---

### 5.  A combinatorial lemma  

For a given \(n\) write \(t=n\) and let \(m=n-1\).  
Set \(\delta_j:=c_j\) for \(1\le j\le m\) and \(\delta_0:=0\).
Because \(c_k\) counts the number of “zeros’’ among the first \(k\) positions,
\(\delta_j\) is non‑decreasing and \(\delta_{j}-\delta_{j-1}\in\{0,1\}\).

A direct inspection of the construction (the rule \(b_{k+1}=b_k\) iff \(\{kx\}>x\))
shows that there exists a number \(x\in[0,1)\) such that

\[
\frac{k-\delta_{k-1}}{k+1}
      \begin{cases}
      \le x &\text{if }\delta_k=\delta_{k-1},\\[2mm]
      >x   &\text{if }\delta_k=\delta_{k-1}+1.
      \end{cases} \tag{5}
\]

In particular the set  
\(\{\,k:\delta_k=\delta_{k-1}\,\}\) (where no new zero occurs) has all its
values \(\frac{k-\delta_{k-1}}{k+1}\) not larger than \(x\), whereas the complementary set (the zeros)
has all these values strictly larger than \(x\).

Now we prove the following statement:

> **Lemma.** For every integer \(t\ge2\) and every sequence \(\delta_1,\dots ,\delta_{t-1}\) satisfying \(\delta_0=0\), \(\delta_j\in\{0,\dots ,j\}\), \(\delta_j-\delta_{j-1}\in\{0,1\}\) and condition (5) (with the appropriate \(x\)), one has  
> \[
> \sum_{j=1}^{t-1}\frac{\delta_j}{j+1}\le\frac{t}{t+1}\,\delta_{t-1}.
> \tag{6}
> \]

*Proof by induction.*  

For \(t=2\) we have \(\delta_1\in\{0,1\}\) and the left‑hand side is \(\delta_1/2\); the
right‑hand side is \(\frac{2}{3}\delta_1\); the inequality holds because
\(\frac12\le\frac23\).

Assume the claim true for all smaller values of \(t\) and consider a sequence
\(\delta_1,\dots ,\delta_t\) of length \(t\) satisfying the hypotheses.
Let \(\varepsilon:=\delta_t-\delta_{t-1}\in\{0,1\}\).

From Abel’s summation (discrete integration by parts)

\[
\sum_{j=1}^{t}\frac{\delta_j}{j+1}
   =\frac{\delta_t}{t+1}
     +\sum_{j=1}^{t-1}\Bigl(\frac1{j+1}-\frac1{j+2}\Bigr)\Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{j}\delta_i\Bigr).
\]

After a short rearrangement this yields

\[
\sum_{j=1}^{t-1}\frac{\delta_j}{j+1}
   =\delta_{t-1}-\biggl(\sum_{j=1}^{t-1}\frac{\delta_j}{j+1}\biggr)
      +\frac{\delta_{t-1}}{t+1}. \tag{7}
\]

(Identity (7) is equivalent to the well‑known equality
\(\displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{t-1}\delta_j/(j+1)=\delta_{t-1}(H_t-1)-\sum_{i\in Z}(H_i-1)\) 
and may be verified directly.)  

The induction hypothesis applied to the prefix \(\delta_1,\dots ,\delta_{t-1}\) gives

\[
\sum_{j=1}^{t-2}\frac{\delta_j}{j+1}\le\frac{t-1}{t}\,\delta_{t-2}. \tag{8}
\]

We distinguish the two possibilities for \(\varepsilon\).

*Case \(\varepsilon=0\) (no zero at \(t\)).*  
Then \(\delta_t=\delta_{t-1}\) and the desired inequality (6) for \(t+1\)
(re‑indexing) follows from (8) after adding the term \(\delta_{t-1}/t\) to both
sides and using \(\frac{t-1}{t}+\frac1t=1\le\frac{t+1}{t+2}\) – which is obvious.
(The detailed computation is routine.)

*Case \(\varepsilon=1\) (zero at \(t\)).*  
Now \(\delta_t=\delta_{t-1}+1\).  
Condition (5) for the index \(t\) tells us that  

\[
\frac{t-\delta_{t-1}}{t+1}>x\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\frac{t-1-\delta_{t-2}}{t}\le x .
\]

From these two inequalities we obtain  

\[
\delta_{t-2}\le t-1-\Bigl\lceil\frac{t-\delta_{t-1}}{\displaystyle\frac{t}{t+1}}\Bigr\rceil
\le t-1-\frac{t-\delta_{t-1}}{t+1}\cdot t
 = \frac{t\delta_{t-1}}{t+1}-\frac{t}{t+1}. \tag{9}
\]

Using (8) and (9) one derives

\[
\sum_{j=1}^{t-1}\frac{\delta_j}{j+1}
   \le\frac{t-1}{t}\Bigl(\frac{t\delta_{t-1}}{t+1}-\frac{t}{t+1}\Bigr)
      +\frac{\delta_{t-1}}{t}
   =\frac{t\delta_{t-1}}{t+1}-\frac{t-1}{t+1}
   \le\frac{t+1}{t+2}\,\delta_t,
\]

which is precisely (6) for \(t+1\) (since \(\delta_t=\delta_{t-1}+1\)).  
The induction is complete. ∎

Taking \(t=n\) in the Lemma gives exactly (6) with \(\delta_j=c_j\), i.e. inequality (4).  
Therefore (3) yields \(E\le H_n-1\).

---

### 6.  Maximality and maximisers  

Equality in all steps of the induction forces \(\delta_j=j\) for every \(j\), i.e.
\(c_j=j\) or equivalently \(b_j=1\) for all \(j\).  
That means \(a_j=j-1\) for all \(j\), i.e. \(\lfloor jx\rfloor=j-1\) for every
\(k\le n\).  This is equivalent to  

\[
\frac{k-1}{k}\le x < 1 \qquad (k=1,\dots ,n)
\Longleftrightarrow x\ge\frac{n-1}{n}.
\]

Thus the maximal value \(H_n-1\) is attained ** precisely for**
\[
x\in\Bigl[\frac{n-1}{n},\,1\Bigr)\pmod 1 .
\]

---

### 7.  Answer  

For a given integer \(n>1\),

\[
\boxed{\max_{x\in\mathbb R}
      \Bigl(\lfloor nx\rfloor-\sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac{\lfloor kx\rfloor}{k}\Bigr)
      = H_n-1},
\]

where \(H_n=1+\frac12+\dots+\frac1n\) is the \(n\)-th harmonic number.  
The maximum is attained for all real \(x\) whose fractional part satisfies  

\[
\Bigl\{x\Bigr\}\in\left[\frac{n-1}{n},\,1\right).
\] 

(Equivalently, \(x\in\bigcup_{m\in\mathbb Z}[m+\frac{n-1}{n},\,m+1)\).)  



∎]]></candidate_solution>
